title: I Tracked the Neighbor's Camera Through Three HOA Hearings

parts.text: A camera on Dale's eave pointed into my bedroom at an angle no package needed. I was forty-three. I asked him to tilt. He said HOA allows security. I measured the angle with a cheap app and brought photos to hearing one. The board said be neighborly. Dale added a second camera. Neighborly doubled.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The board said neighborly; he answered with a second lens.

social.video_title: One eave camera looked into my bedroom and the board shrugged — Part 1/3
social.description: Angle app, packages as an excuse, be neighborly. Then a second camera. Would you have closed the blinds forever?

parts.text: Hearing two, I brought the bylaws on cameras and recording of private interiors. Dale said he only records his driveway. I played ten seconds of my interior lights reflecting in his night shot, which he had posted in the Facebook group as a flex. The board asked him to take the Facebook post down. They did not ask him to tilt. I hired a plastic owl for my sill, which did nothing except make me feel like I had a witness. Dale laughed at the owl in the group.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: They policed the Facebook flex and left the lens on my glass.

social.video_title: He posted my interior lights as a security flex — Part 2/3
social.description: Bylaws, ten seconds of night shot, a plastic owl. Would you have sued instead of a third hearing?

parts.text: Hearing three, the management company's lawyer existed. Lawyers like interiors. The cameras tilted to asphalt. Dale called me obsessed. I called me done. The owl stayed because I like its face. The Facebook group banned security flexes. My bedroom went back to being a room. Three hearings is a stupid number and also the number it took. Asphalt is a reasonable hobby for a lens. People are not.

social.video_title: The lawyer aimed the eaves at asphalt — Part 3/3
social.description: Tilted cameras, owl as decor, banned flexes. Was security a bedroom sport?
